claims.claim: On January twelfth, 2020, Taal Volcano in the Philippines erupted after a 43‑year quiet.
claims.evidence: The volcano erupted on the afternoon of January 12, 2020, 43 years after its previous eruption in 1977.
claims.quote: The volcano erupted on the afternoon of January 12, 2020, 43 years after its previous eruption in 1977.

claims.claim: Seismic swarms began at eleven in the morning, followed by a phreatic blast from the main crater around one o’clock.
claims.evidence: Seismic swarms began at 11 am and were later followed by a phreatic eruption from Volcano Island Main Crater at around 1 pm Philippine Standard Time (UTC+8).
claims.quote: Seismic swarms began at 11 am and were later followed by a phreatic eruption from Volcano Island Main Crater at around 1 pm Philippine Standard Time (UTC+8).

claims.claim: The explosion sent a towering ash column over the surrounding Calabarzon region and even reached Metro Manila.
claims.evidence: a phreatomagmatic eruption from its main crater spewed ashes over Calabarzon, Metro Manila, and some parts of Central Luzon and Ilocos Region
claims.quote: a phreatomagmatic eruption from its main crater spewed ashes over Calabarzon, Metro Manila, and some parts of Central Luzon and Ilocos Region

claims.claim: Ash fell so thick that schools closed, flights were halted, and the lake’s surface temporarily dried, erasing the tiny Vulcan Point island.
claims.evidence: resulting in the suspension of school classes, work schedules, and flights in the area, as well as temporarily drying up Taal Main Crater Lake and destroying Vulcan Point, an Island surrounded by the lake.
claims.quote: resulting in the suspension of school classes, work schedules, and flights in the area, as well as temporarily drying up Taal Main Crater Lake and destroying Vulcan Point, an Island surrounded by the lake.

claims.claim: PHIVOLCS raised the alert to level four, warning that a hazardous eruption could occur within hours to days.
claims.evidence: The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) subsequently issued an Alert Level 4, indicating 'that a hazardous explosive eruption is possible within hours to days.'
claims.quote: The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) subsequently issued an Alert Level 4, indicating 'that a hazardous explosive eruption is possible within hours to days.'

claims.claim: Stronger explosions at three p.m. produced a hundred‑meter ash plume, prompting evacuations of nearby towns.
claims.evidence: Stronger explosions began around 3 pm that spewed an ash column
claims.quote: Stronger explosions began around 3 pm that spewed an ash column

claims.claim: Later, smaller eruptions continued through 2021, and a brief phreatomagmatic burst on March twenty‑six, 2022, lifted the alert to level three.
claims.evidence: Volcanic activity continued into 2021, when smaller eruptions occurred in July 2021. On March 26, 2022, a short-lived phreatomagmatic eruption was recorded by PHIVOLCS raising the status from Alert level 2 to Alert level 3.
claims.quote: Volcanic activity continued into 2021, when smaller eruptions occurred in July 2021. On March 26, 2022, a short-lived phreatomagmatic eruption was recorded by PHIVOLCS raising the status from Alert level 2 to Alert level 3.

claims.claim: These events illustrate how volcanoes at convergent plate boundaries can shift from quiet magma chambers to violent, ash‑filled blasts.
claims.evidence: The source material does not explicitly state that Taal Volcano is at a convergent plate boundary.
